passages.happening:
In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, of the royal family and one of the king's chief officers, comes with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and they eat a meal together there (verse 1). Then Ishmael and his men get up and strike down Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had made governor (verse 2). Ishmael also kills the Judeans with Gedaliah and the Chaldean soldiers there (verse 3).

The next day, before anyone knows, eighty men come from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, in mourning, bringing grain offerings and incense to the house of the LORD (verses 4 and 5). Ishmael goes out weeping to meet them and invites them in to Gedaliah (verse 6). Inside the town he and his men kill them and throw them into a cistern (verse 7). Ten of them save their lives by telling Ishmael they have hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey in the fields (verse 8). The cistern was the one King Asa had made long before against Baasha king of Israel (verse 9).

Ishmael takes captive the rest of the people at Mizpah, including the king's daughters whom Nebuzaradan had put in Gedaliah's care, and sets out to cross over to the Ammonites (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 gives the month but not the year. Many place the murder in the same year Jerusalem fell, only a few months after Gedaliah was appointed. Others think his rule lasted longer. A later fast in the seventh month, mentioned in Zechariah, is traditionally linked with Gedaliah's death.

Ishmael belonged to the royal family, which may explain his motive: a member of David's house might resent a governor from a scribal family serving Babylon. Baalis king of Ammon backed him, probably hoping to keep Judah unsettled. To kill a host after sharing his table was among the worst betrayals the ancient world knew.

The eighty men from the north were mourners coming to the ruined temple site with offerings. Even after the fall, people still came to worship. The chapter tells their killing in a few words, and these notes do the same.
passages.later: Kings tells the same murder in one verse: Ishmael ‘came with ten men and struck down and killed Gedaliah’ (2 Kings 25:25). Zechariah later promises that the fast of the seventh month will become one of the ‘times of joy and gladness’ (Zechariah 8:19).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible record such a senseless atrocity, and why is God silent in this chapter?

There is no word from God in chapter 41, and Jeremiah does not appear. Some readers find that silence troubling. One answer is that biblical narrative often reports evil without comment, trusting the reader to see it for what it is, and the silence itself reflects the chaos after the city fell: without king, temple or a people listening to the prophet, violence filled the gap. Another is that the chapter warned the book's first readers, many of them exiles, of what happens when a community without God's direction turns on itself. The text does not explain why God allowed the pilgrims to die, and it is honest to leave that question open, as the Bible itself does in Job and the lament psalms.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ishmael came weeping and killed those who trusted him. Ask how you would recognize false tears in someone who means harm. And ask how you live faithfully when God seems silent and violence fills the gap.

passages.t: Johanan rescues the captives, and the road toward Egypt
passages.happening:
When Johanan son of Kareah and the commanders with him hear what Ishmael has done (verse 11), they take their men and go after him, and they find him by the great pool in Gibeon (verse 12). The captives see Johanan and rejoice (verse 13). They turn and go over to him (verse 14). But Ishmael and eight men escape to the Ammonites (verse 15).

Johanan and the commanders take the whole remnant they have rescued, soldiers, women, children and court officials (verse 16), and stop at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, on their way to Egypt (verse 17), to escape the Chaldeans. They are afraid, because Ishmael has killed Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon appointed over the land (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The great pool in Gibeon was a known landmark, the same place where David's men and Saul's men once fought (2 Samuel 2).

Johanan rescued the captives, and then fear took over. Babylon would hold someone responsible for the murder of its governor and its soldiers, and the survivors expected reprisal. They began to move toward Egypt before asking God anything.

Bethlehem lay south of Jerusalem on the road to Egypt. The remnant was already on its way. The next chapter tells how they asked Jeremiah for God's word after their minds were made up.
passages.later: The pool of Gibeon was where the men of Abner and Joab met in David's early days (2 Samuel 2:13). Later the returning exiles included the people of Bethlehem (Ezra 2:21).
passages.asks: The survivors were rescued and then ran on in fear. Ask whether you have let fear decide your road before asking God. And ask what it would look like to stop and listen, even after you have already started moving.
